slides.title: Pimpl Idiom (Pointer to Implementation)
slides.prompt: Pimpl hides private implementation members behind a forward-declared pointer, reducing compilation dependencies and build times.

slides.title: Primary Pimpl Idiom Benefit
slides.prompt: What is the key advantage of using the Pimpl idiom in commercial C++ libraries?
options: ABI stability and faster compile times (changes to Impl don't recompile client code)
Faster runtime speed due to extra pointer indirection
Elimination of dynamic heap memory allocation
slides.correctAnswer: ABI stability and faster compile times (changes to Impl don't recompile client code)

slides.title: Pimpl Destructor Requirement
slides.prompt: Why must the destructor of a Pimpl class be defined in the .cpp implementation file rather than header?
options: To ensure Impl type is complete when std::unique_ptr destructor is instantiated
Required by C++ virtual table layout rules
Header destructors automatically inline and fail
To prevent duplicate symbol linker errors
slides.correctAnswer: To ensure Impl type is complete when std::unique_ptr destructor is instantiated

slides.title: Nested Class Outer Scope Access
slides.prompt: Can a nested class access private members of its enclosing (outer) class in modern C++?
options: Yes, nested class has full access rights to enclosing class members
No, nested classes have zero access to outer class members
Only if nested class inherits from outer class
Only if outer class members are static
slides.correctAnswer: Yes, nested class has full access rights to enclosing class members

slides.title: Pimpl Runtime Overhead
slides.prompt: What is the main performance trade-off associated with Pimpl Idiom?
options: Dynamic memory allocation cost and pointer indirection overhead
Cache line eviction during vector sorting
slides.correctAnswer: Dynamic memory allocation cost and pointer indirection overhead
